newsitem.title: USA: Clinton turns attention to staff changes.
newsitem.headline: Clinton turns attention to staff changes.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, basking in the triumph of a re-election win that seemed impossible just two years ago, now turns his attention to staff changes that will shape the direction of his second term.
Still enjoying the raucous celebrations in Little Rock that followed his victory on Tuesday night, Clinton intends to move quickly to make some changes in his Cabinet and White House staff.
Those close to Clinton say the changes will not be sweeping, but they will involve some key players who influenced the president's first four years.
Clinton met privately with Secretary of State Warren Christopher, who played a major role four years ago in advising him on selecting members of his administration.
White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said Clinton considers Christopher "a person who can provide thoughtful counsel on those type of matters."
He said the two also discussed "the secretary's own plans." It has been widely expected that Christopher, who is 71, would not stay on if Clinton won a second term.

McCurry insisted that Clinton has not focused on the makeup of his administration in a second term -- concentrating instead on the task of beating Republican challenger Bob Dole and Reform Party candidate Ross Perot.

The task had been formidable. After the 1994 elections, which saw Republicans win control of the House and Senate for the first time in 40 years, Clinton had been forced to insist he was still "relevant" as many wrote his political obituary.
Now that the man known as the "Comeback Kid" has come back in convincing fashion, he intends to move quickly to make changes that eventually will influence the success or failure of his presidency.
"He has not wrestled some of these questions down," McCurry said in trying to discourage speculation that decisions had already been made.

White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta has said he plans to leave, but no specific time has been set. He has taken the lead on reshuffling the Cabinet, while Evelyn Lieberman, one of his deputies, has been studying key White House jobs for changes.

Panetta on Tuesday told NBC that Republican candidates would be considered. "It is going to be based hopefully on those who are best qualified to serve in those positions, and that could include some Republicans," he said.

Vernon Jordan, a longtime Washington powerbroker, and former White House Deputy Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles also have been tapped to lead transition efforts. Administration officials say Clinton would like to see Bowles, a close friend, replace Panetta but the former government official has resisted the move.

According to individuals close to Clinton, frontrunners to replace Christopher include George Mitchell, former Senate Democratic leader and the president's special envoy on Northern Ireland, U.N. Ambassador Madeleine Albright and Richard Holbrooke, the former assistant secretary of state who brokered the Bosnia peace accord.
Clinton, who was returning to Washington on Wednesday afternoon, planned to meet with his Cabinet to discuss possible changes on Friday, officials said.

Although officials insist there is no immediate deadline on Clinton to act, since his second term does not start until January, several have indicated he would like to announce some decisions before he departs on Tuesday on a lengthy trip that includes a brief vacation in Hawaii followed by visits to the Philippines, Australia and Thailand.
